questions.stem: An IQN is asked to use an unfamiliar electronic medication system independently on the first shift. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Request orientation and supervised practice before independent use.
Proceed because the medication principles are familiar.
Ask a colleague to enter the medicine under their login.

questions.rationale: Safe adaptation requires orientation, supervision and confirmation of competence before independent practice. Previous experience does not replace local system training.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the relationship between organisational policy and professional judgement?

options.text: Professional judgement allows nurses to ignore policy.
Policy provides the local process, while professional judgement remains necessary for individual circumstances.
Policy removes the need to assess the patient.
Professional judgement applies only when no policy exists.

questions.rationale: Policies define approved processes, but nurses must still assess the patient and respond safely when circumstances differ from routine practice.

questions.stem: A busy ward is short-staffed. Which safety behaviour should remain unchanged?

options.text: Completing hand hygiene and patient identification checks.
Skipping aseptic steps for simple procedures.

questions.rationale: Core safety behaviours must remain reliable despite workload pressure. Busy conditions do not justify shortcuts.

questions.stem: An IQN notices that a local isolation procedure differs from previous overseas practice. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow previous practice because it is familiar.
Ask the patient which method to use.
Use the local approved procedure and seek clarification if needed.

questions.rationale: International practice requires adaptation to local standards, policies and equipment while maintaining evidence-based safety principles.

questions.stem: A nurse finds that a commonly used ward practice conflicts with a newly issued guideline. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Review the evidence and raise the issue through organisational governance.
Continue the old practice until an incident occurs.
Ignore the guideline because routines are established.

questions.rationale: Evidence-based change should be considered through approved governance and implementation processes rather than ignored or introduced independently.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates consistent international safety practice?

options.text: Using safety checks only with unfamiliar patients.
Applying identification, allergy and aseptic checks across every shift and setting.
Relaxing checks when working with experienced colleagues.

questions.rationale: Reliable systems depend on consistent behaviour regardless of experience, workload or familiarity.

questions.stem: An IQN has performed implanted port access many times overseas but has not been assessed locally. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Perform it independently because the skill is transferable.
Ask another nurse to sign afterwards.
Request supervised practice and local competency assessment.

questions.rationale: Local competency requirements protect patients and confirm safe use of approved equipment and processes.

questions.stem: Which source should an IQN use FIRST when unsure about a local procedure?

options.text: The current organisational policy or clinical guideline.

questions.rationale: Current organisational policies and guidelines are the primary source for local approved practice.

questions.stem: A nurse says, 'This is how we have always done it.' What is the BEST response?

options.text: Ask whether current evidence and policy support the practice.
Avoid discussing it to preserve teamwork.

questions.rationale: Habit alone is not sufficient. Nurses should compare routine practice with current evidence and policy.

questions.stem: What best demonstrates professionalism when entering a new healthcare system?

options.text: Seeking clarification and supervision when needed.

questions.rationale: Seeking support is a professional safety behaviour, not a weakness.

questions.stem: A local policy is unclear in a high-risk situation. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Escalate for clarification while maintaining immediate patient safety.

questions.rationale: When guidance is unclear, the nurse should protect the patient and seek timely clarification through appropriate channels.

questions.stem: Which practice most strongly supports reliable infection prevention?

options.text: Allowing staff to choose hand hygiene moments individually.
Assuming senior staff need fewer checks.
Standardising key procedures and auditing consistent performance.

questions.rationale: Standardisation and monitoring improve reliability and reduce variation in critical safety processes.

questions.stem: A nurse encounters unfamiliar PPE for an airborne-risk patient. What is the safest response?

options.text: Review the local procedure and seek assistance before entry if time permits safely.
Enter without PPE to avoid delay.
Ask the family to provide care.

questions.rationale: Correct PPE selection and use are essential. The nurse should follow local guidance and seek assistance while ensuring urgent care is not delayed unsafely.

questions.stem: Which statement about international nursing standards is MOST accurate?

options.text: They remove the need for local policies.
They provide broad expectations that are implemented through local procedures.
They are optional for experienced nurses.
They apply only to infection control.

questions.rationale: Professional and regulatory standards establish broad expectations, while organisations translate them into local processes.

questions.stem: An IQN notices that two local policies appear inconsistent. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Ask a senior clinician or governance lead to clarify the current approved process.

questions.rationale: Conflicting guidance should be clarified through appropriate organisational channels before proceeding.

questions.stem: Why is orientation to local equipment important?

options.text: Orientation is required only for students.
Equipment design and safety features may differ between systems.

questions.rationale: Different devices may have unique settings, alarms and risks; orientation reduces avoidable harm.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to bypass a new electronic identification step because it slows workflow. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use the approved process and raise workflow concerns through proper channels.
Skip it only for familiar patients.
Ask another nurse to take responsibility.

questions.rationale: Safety requirements should not be bypassed. Workflow issues should be addressed through system improvement, not unsafe shortcuts.

questions.stem: Which action best supports evidence into practice?

options.text: Reading a new guideline but changing nothing.
Participating in education and applying the approved updated process.
Relying on memory from years ago.

questions.rationale: Evidence translation requires education, implementation and ongoing use in practice.

questions.stem: A nurse is competent in a procedure but unfamiliar with the local documentation system. What should happen?

options.text: Documentation can be added days later.
Another nurse may document without observing.
The procedure may proceed only if documentation can be completed safely according to policy.
Documentation is optional if the skill is performed correctly.

questions.rationale: Safe care includes accurate, timely documentation. If the nurse cannot complete this safely, support is required.

questions.stem: Which outcome BEST indicates successful adaptation by an IQN?

options.text: The nurse follows previous practice unchanged.
The nurse depends on colleagues for all decisions.
The nurse applies local policies consistently while using sound clinical judgement.

questions.rationale: Successful transition combines adaptation to local systems with professional judgement and accountability.

questions.stem: A patient's respiratory rate rises from 18 to 30 breaths per minute over two hours. What should the nurse do FIRST?

options.text: Assess the patient immediately and review the observation trend.
Document the change for the next shift.
Wait for blood pressure to fall.

questions.rationale: A rising respiratory rate is an early sign of deterioration and requires immediate assessment and escalation as indicated.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes dynamic risk assessment?

options.text: Risk is assessed once at admission.
Risk is reassessed when condition, treatment or environment changes.

questions.rationale: Risk changes over time and should be reassessed when relevant circumstances change.

questions.stem: A patient is newly confused, febrile and passing little urine. What is the PRIORITY interpretation?

options.text: Possible infection and deterioration requiring urgent assessment.

questions.rationale: New confusion, fever and reduced urine output may indicate serious infection or sepsis.

questions.stem: A patient's early warning score is below the trigger threshold, but the nurse believes the patient is deteriorating. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Escalate based on clinical concern and provide objective findings.

questions.rationale: Structured scores support but do not replace clinical judgement. Concern should be escalated when the clinical picture is worrying.

questions.stem: Which part of ISBAR contains the nurse's clinical findings?
questions.rationale: The Assessment component communicates current findings and the nurse's clinical interpretation.

questions.stem: A family member says, 'He is not himself today,' although vital signs are near baseline. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Reassure the family and continue routine care.
Take the concern seriously and reassess the patient.

questions.rationale: Families may identify subtle changes before objective deterioration becomes obvious.

questions.stem: A patient becomes dizzy after a new antihypertensive medication. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Medication changes can alter falls risk; reassessment is required before activity.

questions.stem: Which finding requires the MOST urgent escalation?

options.text: New reduction in level of consciousness.

questions.rationale: Altered consciousness may indicate serious deterioration and requires urgent review.

questions.stem: A patient on oxygen has saturation of 84%. What is the BEST initial action?

options.text: Assess the patient and oxygen delivery system while initiating escalation.

questions.rationale: Immediate assessment of the patient and equipment is required because severe hypoxaemia may be life-threatening.

questions.stem: Escalation has been initiated, but the response is delayed and the patient worsens. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue escalation through the next approved level while providing ongoing care.

questions.rationale: Escalation should continue until the response matches the urgency of the situation.

questions.stem: Which trend is MOST concerning after surgery?

options.text: Stable pain score and urine output.
Falling blood pressure with rising pulse.

questions.rationale: Falling blood pressure and rising pulse may indicate bleeding or shock.

questions.stem: A patient has a normal blood pressure but new tachypnoea and confusion. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: The combined changes require urgent reassessment.

questions.rationale: Deterioration may be present despite one normal observation. Trends and combined findings matter.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of structured risk tools?

options.text: To support consistent recognition and communication of risk.

questions.rationale: Risk tools support, but do not replace, clinical judgement.

questions.stem: A nurse identifies increasing pain despite analgesia. What is the BEST action?
questions.rationale: Persistent or increasing pain may indicate complications and requires reassessment.

questions.stem: Which ISBAR statement is the strongest recommendation?

options.text: 'Please review the patient urgently because of new confusion, RR 32 and oxygen saturation 88%.'

questions.rationale: A strong recommendation clearly states the requested action and the clinical reasons.

questions.stem: A patient becomes pale and sweaty on standing. What should the nurse do FIRST?

options.text: Assist the patient to a safe position and assess.

questions.rationale: Immediate safety and assessment are priorities when instability occurs.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates prioritisation?

options.text: Assessing sudden chest pain and breathlessness before non-urgent requests.
Completing routine documentation before assessing chest pain.
Answering all call bells in order received.

questions.rationale: Potentially life-threatening airway, breathing and circulation concerns take priority.

questions.stem: A patient is deteriorating after a procedure. Which information is MOST important during escalation?

options.text: Current observations, changes from baseline, interventions and response.

questions.rationale: Escalation should include objective, relevant clinical data and the response to interventions.

questions.stem: Why should reduced urine output be escalated?

options.text: It is always normal after surgery.
It may indicate reduced perfusion or organ dysfunction.
It is less important than temperature.

questions.rationale: Falling urine output may indicate reduced renal perfusion or systemic deterioration.

questions.stem: Which outcome best shows effective early escalation?

options.text: The patient received timely review and treatment before severe deterioration.

questions.rationale: The purpose of escalation is timely intervention that prevents worsening harm.

questions.stem: During handover, which information is MOST important?

options.text: Current condition, recent changes, risks and required actions.
All notes read word for word.

questions.rationale: Effective handover prioritises clinically relevant information and outstanding actions.

questions.stem: Which documentation entry is most appropriate?

options.text: 'Patient declined shower, stating fatigue; education provided and plan reviewed.'

questions.rationale: Documentation should be objective, factual and describe what occurred and what action was taken.

questions.stem: A nurse receives a telephone order that sounds unclear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use closed-loop read-back and follow policy.

questions.rationale: Read-back confirms accuracy and reduces communication errors.

questions.stem: What should happen FIRST after a medication incident?
questions.rationale: Immediate patient care takes priority before reporting and review.

questions.stem: A near miss causes no harm. Why should it still be reported?

options.text: To identify system weaknesses before harm occurs.
Because all staff must be blamed.

questions.rationale: Near misses are valuable learning opportunities that reveal latent risks.

questions.stem: Which statement about incident reports is correct?

options.text: They complement but do not replace clinical documentation.
They are completed only if injury occurs.

questions.rationale: Clinical documentation records care; incident reports support organisational learning.

questions.stem: A receiving nurse does not understand an outstanding action during handover. What should happen?

options.text: Ask for clarification and confirm who will act.

questions.rationale: Handover should allow questions and clear transfer of responsibility.

questions.stem: A nurse documents before providing care. Why is this unsafe?

options.text: It is acceptable for routine care.
It may create a false record if care changes or is not completed.

questions.rationale: Documentation should reflect actual care provided, not intended future actions.

questions.stem: Which statement best demonstrates closed-loop communication in an emergency?

options.text: 'Give 5 mg morphine IV now.' '5 mg morphine IV now.' 'Correct.'

questions.rationale: The receiver repeats the message and the sender confirms it, reducing misunderstanding.

questions.stem: A patient deteriorates rapidly. What should the nurse document?

options.text: Assessment findings, times, interventions, responses and notifications.

questions.rationale: Comprehensive, time-based documentation supports continuity, accountability and review.

questions.stem: Which phrase should be avoided in professional documentation?
questions.rationale: Labels such as 'non-compliant' are subjective and should be replaced with objective descriptions.

questions.stem: An incident report asks for contributing factors. Which response is BEST?

options.text: State only who made the error.
Describe workload, interruptions, equipment and communication factors factually.

questions.rationale: Incident review should examine factual contributing conditions, not assign blame.

questions.stem: A critical laboratory result is telephoned to the ward. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Repeat the result back, document it and notify the appropriate clinician promptly.

questions.rationale: Critical results require read-back, timely documentation and escalation.

questions.stem: During handover, the outgoing nurse says a patient is 'fine.' What should the receiving nurse do?

options.text: Request objective observations, recent changes and outstanding risks.

questions.rationale: Vague handover is unsafe; objective information is required.

questions.stem: A nurse discovers an error in the electronic record. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Ask another nurse to change it.
Correct it according to policy while preserving the audit trail.

questions.rationale: Corrections must follow legal and organisational requirements and maintain transparency.

questions.stem: Why should responsibility be confirmed at handover?

options.text: To prevent important actions from being assumed or omitted.

questions.rationale: Clear ownership reduces missed care and communication failures.

questions.stem: A nurse reports a near miss but omits it from team review. What learning opportunity is lost?

options.text: The chance to identify patterns and prevent recurrence.

questions.rationale: Near misses can reveal system weaknesses and trends before patients are harmed.

questions.stem: Which handover format best supports safety?

options.text: Prioritised ISBAR with opportunity for questions.

questions.rationale: Structured handover improves clarity and continuity.

questions.stem: A nurse documents 'doctor informed' without details. What is missing?

options.text: The clinician's name, time, information communicated and response or plan.

questions.rationale: Documentation should clearly identify who was informed, when, what was communicated and the resulting plan.

questions.stem: Which outcome BEST reflects effective communication and incident management?

options.text: Risks are clearly communicated, patient care is protected and system learning occurs.

questions.rationale: Effective management combines immediate safety, accurate communication and organisational learning.

questions.stem: A patient with limited English needs discharge education about wound care. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use a professional interpreter and teach-back.
Ask a child family member to translate.

questions.rationale: Professional interpretation and teach-back support accurate, safe communication.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of teach-back?

options.text: To confirm whether the explanation was understood.

questions.rationale: Teach-back checks the effectiveness of the nurse's explanation.

questions.stem: A patient asks whether the nurse cleaned their hands. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Tell the patient not to question staff.
Acknowledge the question and perform hand hygiene if needed.

questions.rationale: Patients should be invited to participate in safety, including hand hygiene awareness.

questions.stem: A family member offers to interpret a complex consent discussion. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use the family member because it is quicker.
Arrange a qualified interpreter while allowing family support.

questions.rationale: Qualified interpreters improve accuracy, confidentiality and informed decision-making.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates cultural safety?

options.text: Asking the patient what matters to them and adapting care where safe.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety requires respectful enquiry and avoidance of stereotypes.

questions.stem: A cultural preference conflicts with a non-negotiable infection-control requirement. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain the safety requirement respectfully and explore acceptable alternatives.

questions.rationale: The nurse should balance cultural respect with evidence-based safety and seek alternatives where possible.

questions.stem: A patient with hearing impairment receives safety instructions. What is the BEST method?

options.text: Face the patient, use accessible written or visual support and confirm understanding.

questions.rationale: Communication should be adapted to the patient's needs and verified.

questions.stem: Which patient action should nurses encourage as part of shared safety?

options.text: Confirming identity and reporting allergies or changes.

questions.rationale: Patients can contribute meaningfully by confirming identity, reporting allergies and describing changes.

questions.stem: A patient nods throughout education but cannot explain the plan. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: The explanation should be adapted and repeated using teach-back.

questions.rationale: Nodding does not prove understanding. Teaching should be adapted and checked.

questions.stem: A patient with low health literacy needs medication instructions. What is BEST?

options.text: Use plain language, visual aids and teach-back.
Ask the patient to search online.

questions.rationale: Accessible communication improves safety and self-management.

questions.stem: A patient refuses a safety intervention because of a previous traumatic healthcare experience. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore concerns, explain options and use a trauma-informed approach.

questions.rationale: Trauma-informed care supports safety through choice, explanation and respectful engagement.

questions.stem: Which action best preserves patient autonomy during safety planning?

options.text: Make the plan without the patient.
Use restriction as the first option.
Ask family to decide without consent.
Discuss risks and agree on practical strategies with the patient.

questions.rationale: Shared decision-making improves engagement and respects autonomy.

questions.stem: A patient with visual impairment must learn drain care. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use tactile demonstration, verbal explanation and return demonstration.
Ask the family to do everything.

questions.rationale: Education should be adapted to sensory needs and confirmed through performance.

questions.stem: A patient prefers a traditional practice that does not create clinical risk. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to adopt local customs.

questions.rationale: Safe cultural preferences should be respected and incorporated where possible.

questions.stem: Which response best invites patient participation in infection prevention?

options.text: 'You may remind us about hand hygiene and tell us if your dressing changes.'

questions.rationale: Inviting participation helps patients contribute to safe care.

questions.stem: A patient cannot read the discharge sheet. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the patient to sign anyway.
Provide verbal and visual education and confirm understanding.

questions.rationale: Education must be accessible and comprehension verified.

questions.stem: A nurse assumes that a patient will refuse blood products based on cultural background. Why is this unsafe?

options.text: It relies on stereotyping rather than individual assessment.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety requires asking individual preferences rather than making assumptions.

questions.stem: A patient with cognitive impairment needs safety education. What is the BEST plan?

options.text: Use simple repeated information, involve appropriate support and assess capacity and understanding.

questions.rationale: Communication should be adapted to cognition while preserving participation and support.

questions.stem: Which outcome BEST indicates effective teach-back?

options.text: The nurse finishes the education quickly.
The patient accurately explains or demonstrates the safety steps in their own words.

questions.rationale: Teach-back is successful when the patient can explain or demonstrate the plan accurately.

questions.stem: What best defines patient-centred safety care?

options.text: Allowing all preferences regardless of risk.
Combining evidence-based safety with individual communication, culture, preferences and participation.

questions.rationale: Patient-centred safety integrates evidence with the person's needs, values and involvement.
